article.title: Why Cash Flow Can Weaken While Profit Grows
article.why: 理解利潤與現金流的時間差，並用運轉資本解釋成長企業的資金壓力。
article.author: OpenAI learning editor

paragraphs.en:
A company can report higher profit and still have less cash available. This surprises people because profit and cash are often treated as if they move together. They do not. Profit is an accounting measure based on when revenue and expenses are recognized. Cash flow depends on when money actually enters and leaves the bank account.

Imagine a business that sells more products this year. Revenue rises, and the income statement shows a higher operating profit. However, many customers are allowed to pay sixty days later. Sales are recorded now, but the cash has not arrived yet. Accounts receivable grows. The company looks more profitable, but part of that profit is still waiting to be collected.

Inventory can create a similar gap. A retailer may buy extra stock before a busy season. The purchase uses cash immediately, but the inventory is not fully recognized as an expense until the products are sold. If inventory rises faster than sales, cash can be tied up even while reported profit improves.

Payment timing on the other side matters too. Accounts payable represents money the company owes suppliers. If suppliers allow longer payment terms, the company can temporarily keep more cash. If payment terms become shorter, cash may leave faster even if profit is unchanged. This is why working capital often explains the difference between profit growth and operating cash flow.

Fast-growing companies are especially exposed. Growth may require more inventory, larger receivables, new staff, or advance payments to suppliers. The business can be economically healthy and still experience a financing squeeze because cash must be invested before customers pay. In extreme cases, a profitable company can face serious liquidity problems.

Managers therefore need to ask more than, “Did profit increase?” They should examine operating cash flow, accounts receivable days, inventory days, and accounts payable days. A useful bridge is the cash conversion cycle, which summarizes how long cash is committed between paying suppliers and collecting from customers.

Quality of growth also matters. If revenue increases mainly because the company offers very generous payment terms, profit may rise while collection risk grows. If inventory rises because products are not selling, the cash problem may signal weak demand rather than healthy expansion. The same accounting movement can have different business meanings.

A practical review starts by reconciling profit to cash. Which items increased profit without bringing in cash? Which items used cash but have not yet become expenses? Did customer payment behavior change? Did the company build inventory deliberately, or did stock accumulate unexpectedly? These questions explain the mechanism instead of treating cash flow as a separate mystery.

The key lesson is simple: profit measures economic performance under accounting rules, while cash flow measures liquidity. A strong business needs both. Profit tells you whether the model can create value; cash tells you whether the company can continue paying employees, suppliers, lenders, and taxes while that value is being realized.

This distinction is also important when comparing companies. Two firms with the same profit margin may have very different cash profiles if one collects immediately and the other waits months for payment. Capital-light subscription businesses may convert profit to cash quickly, while manufacturers or wholesalers often need significant working capital. That does not automatically make one better, but it changes financing needs and risk.

For planning, the trend matters more than one quarter. A temporary inventory build may be normal before a launch. Repeated deterioration in receivable collection or inventory turnover is more concerning. Analysts should therefore connect cash movements to operational reasons and expected timing, not judge them in isolation.
paragraphs.zh: 利潤與現金不是同一件事。應收帳款、庫存與應付帳款的時間差，會讓公司在利潤成長時反而消耗現金。快速成長企業尤其容易出現這種情況，因為往往要先備貨、投入人力或支付供應商，之後才收到客戶款項。分析時應把 profit reconciliation 到 operating cash flow，並檢查 receivable days、inventory days、payable days 與 cash conversion cycle。
paragraphs.ja: 利益が増えても現金が増えるとは限りません。売掛金、在庫、買掛金のタイミング差によって、成長企業ほど先に資金を投入し、後から回収する構造になりやすいからです。利益から営業キャッシュフローへの差を確認し、売掛金日数・在庫日数・買掛金日数やキャッシュ・コンバージョン・サイクルを見ると原因を説明しやすくなります。

grammar.title: even while
grammar.body: 表示兩個看似矛盾的狀況同時成立，例如 cash weakens even while profit grows。

business.explanation: 直接詢問利潤與現金流差異來源。
business.example: What is driving the profit-to-cash gap this quarter?

business.explanation: 判斷資金占用是否為策略性成長投入。
business.example: Is this working-capital build intentional or a sign of slower collection?

quiz.question: Why can profit rise before cash arrives?
quiz.answer: Because revenue can be recognized before customers actually pay.

quiz.question: What three working-capital items should you inspect?
quiz.answer: Accounts receivable, inventory, and accounts payable.
